newsitem.title: CHINA: China academic calls for democratic reforms.
newsitem.headline: China academic calls for democratic reforms.

text.p: A Chinese academic has issued a bold but lone call for Western-style democratic reforms ahead of a crucial Communist Party congress.

Beijing University economics professor Shang Dewen said on Thursday he had sent a copy of his blueprint for democracy to Communist Party boss Jiang Zemin, urging the introduction of direct elections for state president and for provincial governors.
"Politically, we have adopted the Stalin model," Shang said in an interview. "Economically, we have adopted the U.S. model."
"The two contradict each other... Reform is needed," the 64-year-old academic said.

China abandoned Soviet-style central planning and embraced market reforms almost two decades ago, but the Communist Party has maintained an iron grip on power, swiftly crushing calls for political change by dissidents.
Shang said he made public his proposal for democratic changes in answer to Jiang's call last May for political reforms.

"It is an undeniable fact that reform of the political system has seriously fallen behind," he wrote in his proposal, in which he urged direct elections of the state president for a maximum of two four-year terms.
However, Shang stressed that his proposal for reform did not encompass a move to change the leadership of the Communist Party.
Asked if he expected the party that has ruled China since 1949 to heed his proposal, Shang said: "The possibility is not big... It's hard to say how long the wait would be."

His proposal was timed to reach China's communist leaders before they hold a party congress in late September or early October to set the path of the world's most populous nation into the 21st century. The congress is held every five years.
Shang said he was not afraid, but added that repercussions to his suggestions could not be ruled out.
"China is a society ruled by man. It's possible," he said when asked if he expected to get into trouble for his call for democratic reforms.
"I'm not worried. Marx, Lenin, Deng Xiaoping and Mao Zedong are gods who will protect me," he said of the icons of communism.

Shang said he differed from China's tiny band of dissidents who have also advocated democratic change. "I'm different from them. They advocate overthrowing the Communist Party. I'm for the Communist Party." he said.
"I'm absolutely not opposed to the Communist Party," said Shang, a party member since 1947.
Most members of China's small group of dissidents who support democratic change are either serving long jail terms or have fled into exile.
